title: The midwife's public health role and epidemiology
blurb: Read maternity data accurately, explain risk in numbers women understand, and use every contact to protect lifelong health.
question: A woman reads that 'Black women are nearly three times more likely to die in pregnancy' and asks her midwife what that means for her. How should the midwife interpret and explain the data?

teach.body: Formally, midwives understand women's lived experience and enable access to public health, social care and community resources; interpret epidemiological data and evidence; share health information so women make evidence-informed decisions; and understand the importance of birth to public health across the life course (SPM 3.1-3.5). In plain English: you read the numbers, translate them honestly, and use pregnancy as a window to improve two lives at once.

teach.caption: Deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days; 24 coincidental deaths are excluded from the rate.

teach.h: Reading a risk ratio and its confidence interval
teach.body: A risk ratio (RR) compares two groups' rates: RR 2.72 means Black women's rate was 2.72 times White women's. The 95% confidence interval shows the plausible range. If it includes 1 (no difference), the result is not statistically significant: Asian women's RR 1.27 (95% CI 0.86-1.84) was not significant, while Black women's RR 2.72 (1.80-4.00) was.

teach.body: Midwife Ola explains to Precious that maternal death is rare: about 13 women per 100,000 maternities across the UK. The 'nearly three times' figure is a relative risk showing a real, significant inequality for Black women. Ola explains that the service takes this seriously: she will listen to Precious's concerns, act early on warning symptoms such as breathlessness or chest pain, and make sure Precious knows how to reach help day and night.

teach.text: A large relative risk can still be a small absolute risk, and a relative risk alone frightens or falsely reassures. Also check the confidence interval: an RR above 1 is not significant if its interval includes 1.

steps.label: Pregnancy
steps.sub: Pertussis from 16 weeks, flu, RSV from 28

items: SPM 3.1-3.5: lived experience, data interpretation, health information, birth and the life course.
MBRRACE 2022-24: 12.80 per 100,000 maternities; VTE leads to 6 weeks, suicide leads 6 weeks to a year.
A risk ratio is significant when its 95% CI does not include 1.
Explain risk with absolute numbers and natural frequencies, not relative risk alone.
Connect women to resources such as Healthy Start, and use every contact for prevention.

summary: You can now interpret maternal mortality data, risk ratios and confidence intervals, and explain risk to women in absolute terms. You can also link public health actions in pregnancy to lifelong health and to the resources women can access.

A.q: According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, what was the leading cause of maternal death during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after?
options: Cardiac disease and cardiomyopathy
Maternal suicide
Thrombosis and thromboembolism
Sepsis from pregnancy infection
A.why: Thrombosis and thromboembolism remained the leading cause during or up to six weeks after the end of pregnancy, followed by cardiac disease and psychiatric causes.

whyNot.0: Cardiac disease was the second most common cause.
whyNot.1: Suicide leads from 6 weeks to 1 year after pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Sepsis was not the leading cause in this period.

A.q: According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, what was the leading cause of maternal death between 6 weeks and 1 year after the end of pregnancy?
options: Thromboembolism
Haemorrhage
Cardiac disease
Maternal suicide
A.why: Maternal suicide remained the leading cause of late maternal deaths, occurring between six weeks and one year after the end of pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Thromboembolism leads in pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after.
whyNot.1: Haemorrhage was not the leading late cause.
whyNot.2: Cardiac disease is second in the earlier period.

A.q: MBRRACE-UK reports a UK maternal death rate of 12.80. What is the denominator for this rate?
options: Per 100,000 maternities
Per 1,000 live births
Per 100,000 women aged 15-44
Per 10,000 births
A.why: The rate was 252 deaths among 1,969,321 maternities: 12.80 per 100,000 maternities.

whyNot.1: Per 1,000 live births is used for some infant measures, not this maternal rate.
whyNot.2: The denominator is maternities, not all women of reproductive age.
whyNot.3: A per 10,000 denominator would give a different figure.

B.q: MBRRACE-UK reports Asian women's risk of maternal death compared with White women as RR 1.27 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.84). How should this be interpreted?
options: Significant, because the risk ratio is above 1
Not significant, because the interval includes 1
Significant, because the upper limit exceeds 1.5
Asian women's risk is 27 times that of White women
B.why: A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 (no difference) means the result is not statistically significant, as MBRRACE states.

whyNot.0: A ratio above 1 is not significant if the interval includes 1.
whyNot.2: The upper limit alone does not determine significance.

B.q: Hannah, expecting her first baby, asks about the risk to her baby of planning a home birth. Which explanation best follows NICE guidance on communicating risk?
options: 'Home birth nearly doubles the risk to your baby.'
'Home birth is unsafe for women having a first baby.'
'About 9 in 1,000 babies at home, 5 in 1,000 elsewhere.'
'The risk to your baby is the same in every setting.'
B.why: NG197 recommends absolute risk and natural frequencies with the same denominator. NG235 data: about 9 per 1,000 for planned home birth vs 5 per 1,000 in other settings for nulliparous women.

whyNot.0: Relative risk alone exaggerates or obscures the absolute difference.
whyNot.1: This is a judgement; birth is generally very safe and she may choose home.
whyNot.3: For first babies, home carries a small increase in risk.

B.q: Which public health action does Saving Babies' Lives version 3 expect for every pregnant woman at booking?
options: Carbon monoxide testing
Weighing at every appointment
An HbA1c blood test
A vitamin A supplement
B.why: SBL v3 element 1: offer CO testing to all women at booking and at 36 weeks, with opt-out referral for a reading of 4 ppm or above.

whyNot.1: NG247 advises against routine weighing throughout pregnancy without a clinical reason.
whyNot.2: HbA1c is not used to assess gestational diabetes risk (NG3).
whyNot.3: Supplements containing vitamin A (retinol) should be avoided in pregnancy (NG247).

C.q: Rani, 23, receives Universal Credit and says she cannot afford pregnancy vitamins. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Suggest cod liver oil capsules as a cheap source
Advise that a varied diet supplies enough vitamin D
Suggest an ordinary multivitamin from the supermarket
Check Healthy Start eligibility and explain how to apply
C.why: NG247 1.1.11: explain how to obtain Healthy Start vitamins free or at low cost and who is eligible; they contain 400 micrograms folic acid and vitamins C and D.

whyNot.0: Cod liver oil contains vitamin A and should not be taken in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: NICE advises a vitamin D supplement because diet and sunlight are often not enough.
whyNot.2: Regular multivitamins may contain retinol (vitamin A), which should be avoided.

C.q: A local audit shows women from the most deprived postcodes book much later than others. Which response best reflects the midwife's public health role?
options: Send reminder letters in English to all late bookers
Discharge women who miss their booking appointment
Work with community partners on outreach booking
Wait for national guidance before changing practice
C.why: SPM 2.8-2.9 and 3.2: use data to inform action, reach out to women who find services hard to access and work with agencies and communities. CG110 1.3.5 supports information in community settings.

whyNot.0: English-only letters may widen the gap they aim to close.
whyNot.1: Discharge deepens the inequality the audit found.
whyNot.3: Local data should drive local action now.

C.q: Rina is 18 weeks pregnant and asks when she can have the whooping cough (pertussis) vaccine. What should the midwife advise?
options: From 16 weeks, ideally around 20 weeks
From 28 weeks, alongside the RSV vaccine
After 32 weeks, as close to birth as possible
In her first pregnancy, not in later ones
C.why: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks, normally around the mid-pregnancy scan (about 20 weeks), ideally before 32 weeks, in every pregnancy.

whyNot.1: 28 weeks is the RSV timing, not the earliest pertussis timing.
whyNot.2: Ideally it is given before 32 weeks for best passive protection.
whyNot.3: It is offered in every pregnancy.

reteach.title: Numbers you can say out loud
reteach.question: How do you turn a frightening headline into something a woman can use?

blocks.body: How many out of how many? (the absolute risk and denominator). Compared with whom? (the relative risk). How sure are we? (the confidence interval: does it include 1?). Then say what you will do about it: listen, act early on warning signs, and connect her to support.

blocks.text: RR 1.27 means 27% higher, not 27 times higher.

explain.body: SPM 3.1: understand women's everyday lives and enable access to public health, social care and community resources. Practical examples: Healthy Start vitamins and food support (NG247), stop-smoking services, domestic abuse support, housing and benefits advice.

test.q: What do Healthy Start vitamins for pregnant or breastfeeding women contain, according to NICE NG247?
options: Folic acid 5 mg with vitamins A and D
Iron and vitamin B12 with vitamin C
Vitamins A, C and D as liquid drops
Folic acid 400 micrograms, vitamins C and D
test.why: NG247 1.1.11: Healthy Start vitamins for pregnant or breastfeeding women contain 400 micrograms folic acid and vitamins C and D.

whyNot.0: 5 mg is the high-dose prescription, and vitamin A is avoided in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: This is not the Healthy Start formulation.
whyNot.2: Vitamins A, C and D drops are the children's product.

explain.body: Rates need a numerator and denominator: 252 deaths per 1,969,321 maternities = 12.80 per 100,000. Risk ratios compare groups; the 95% CI shows certainty. Leading causes: VTE (to 6 weeks), suicide (6 weeks to 1 year).

test.q: A risk ratio of 2.72 for Black women compared with White women means what?
options: Black women's rate was 2.72 times White women's
Black women's rate was 2.72 per 100,000
272 more Black women died than White women
Black women's rate was 2.72% higher
test.why: A risk ratio divides one group's rate by the other's: 2.72 means the rate is 2.72 times as high.

whyNot.1: A ratio is not itself a rate per 100,000.
whyNot.2: A ratio does not express a difference in numbers of deaths.
whyNot.3: 2.72% higher would be a ratio of about 1.03.

explain.body: NICE NG197: present absolute risk using natural frequencies, the same denominator and time period, and both positive and negative framing. Avoid relative risk alone. Check understanding, for example with teach-back.

test.q: Which way of describing risk does NICE NG197 recommend?
options: Relative risk given on its own
Absolute risk as natural frequencies
Odds ratios from the research studies
Descriptive words such as 'rare'
test.why: NG197 1.4.7-1.4.11: use absolute risk and natural frequencies, with consistent denominators and time periods.

whyNot.0: Relative risk alone can mislead about the size of a risk.
whyNot.2: Odds ratios are hard for most people to interpret.
whyNot.3: NG197 recommends numerical, absolute risk rather than descriptive words alone.

explain.body: SPM 3.5: birth matters to public health across the life course. Folic acid prevents neural tube defects; stopping smoking and avoiding alcohol protect the baby; vaccines in pregnancy protect newborns; breastfeeding benefits both woman and baby (NG194 1.5.2).

test.q: At what reading does SBL v3 recommend opt-out referral to a tobacco dependence adviser after CO testing?
options: 2 ppm or above
4 ppm or above
10 ppm or above
15 ppm or above
test.why: SBL v3 element 1: opt-out referral for an elevated CO reading of 4 ppm or above, self-identified smokers, or those who quit in the last 2 weeks.

whyNot.0: 2 ppm is below the referral threshold.
whyNot.2: Over 10 ppm in a non-smoker prompts CO poisoning advice, not the referral threshold.
whyNot.3: 15 ppm is far above the 4 ppm threshold.
